text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton's appointment of Madeleine Albright as secretary of state on Thursday had women's leaders wildly applauding what several termed a historic breakthrough for American women.
"What we've seen today is definitely a glass ceiling being shattered," said Ellen Malcolm, chairwoman of Emily's List, an organisation that raises funds to help women get elected to political office.
"I'm just thrilled. I'm grinning like the Cheshire Cat, I'm so happy," Malcolm said.
Women leaders stressed that Albright got the job on merit but said the fact that she was a woman might have helped her edge out some of her male rivals.
"She didn't get it because she was a woman. She got it because she's qualified. But having said that, this is huge for women all over the world," said Democratic political consultant Jennifer Laszlo.
Clinton himself stressed the same point. "I am very proud to have had the opportunity to appoint the first woman secretary of state in the history of America," he said.

"But it had nothing to do with her getting the job, one way or the other. She got the job because I believe, amid a list of truly outstanding people, she had the best combination of qualities to succeed and to serve our country at this moment in history," Clinton said.
"And I hope that she will be an inspiration to young women all across our country, all across our world," he added.
While few questioned Albright's qualifications, several prominent women leaders said the appointment would also help Clinton politically.

"President Clinton has been the best president in history in terms of recognising and promoting women to important positions. Now, finally, we have one at the highest level inside the inner circle," said Donna Lenhoff, general counsel of the Woman's Defence Fund.
"Clinton won the votes of women partly because he took concrete steps to promote the interests of women and families. And appointing qualified women to top positions is part of that," she said.
In last month's presidential election, Clinton won the women's vote by 16 percentage points, while trailing by one point among men -- a 17 point gender gap.

Last week, a delegation of women met Vice President Al Gore and presented him with a list of 40 women within the administration whom they said should be promoted to more senior positions. Albright's name topped the list.

"This is not a token appointment and it comes at a time when women are being oppressed in some parts of the world more than ever," said Rosemary Dempsey, national vice president of the National Organisation of Women.
"It's historic and it sends an international signal," she said.
Jane Tobler of the Business and Professional Women's Foundation said the appointment could also have an effect in the male-dominated corporate world.

"It will inspire women working in companies and young girls in their classrooms. Up until now, we have preached the gospel of women's equality but we have not been willing to walk the walk," she said.
